title: Who am I? (Exodus 3:11, 4:10–17)
hookLine: Moses protests that he is slow of speech; Aaron will speak for him
last: I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE.

lines: ME? I'M NOT THE RIGHT PERSON.
A BURNING BUSH, A HUGE JOB.
MOSES TRIES TO GET OUT OF IT.
cards: Someone gets offered something big: a promotion, a speech at a wedding, a role they never imagined. And before they even think, the words come out: me? Oh, no.
I'm not the right person. Moses is standing at a burning bush, being told by God himself to go and free a nation of slaves. And he spends most of the conversation trying to get out of it.

teach.b: His first objection is the biggest: "Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh?" A shepherd. A fugitive.
A man who ran away. God doesn't argue with him about who he is.
God says: "Certainly I will be with thee." In Hebrew, ki ehyeh imach. There's yesterday's word: ehyeh, I will be.
The answer to who am I is: it's not only about you. Moses keeps going. What if they ask your name?
What if they don't believe me? Each time, God answers.

teach.h: SLOW OF SPEECH, SLOW OF TONGUE.
teach.b: Then Moses gets personal: "I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue." I'm not a speaker. Never have been.
Nobody knows exactly what he means. A stammer? Rusty Hebrew after years in a palace, or rusty Egyptian after years in the desert?
A midrash tells that as a baby in Pharaoh's house, he burned his tongue on a coal. The Torah doesn't explain. God answers with a question: "Who hath made man's mouth?"
I'll be with your mouth. Finally Moses just says it: please, send someone else. And God is angry; the text says so.

But God doesn't take the job away, and doesn't pretend the weakness isn't real. Your brother Aaron is coming to meet you, God says, and he speaks well. He'll be your mouth, and you'll tell him what to say.
So the man the Torah later calls a prophet like no other didn't think he could speak, and needed his brother's help to do it. The weakness stayed.
He was sent anyway, and not alone.

how: Jewish tradition calls Moses the greatest of the prophets and also the humblest of men, and teachers often point to his reluctance at the bush as part of why he was chosen.

o: slow of speech: a heavy mouth and tongue
I will be: God's promise to be with Moses
a prophet: one who speaks for another

games.q: Moses' objections and God's answers — tap the pairs.

s: God took the job away when Moses objected
God was angry, but still sent him, with Aaron to help.
the Torah explains exactly what slow of speech means
it doesn't. a stammer, a forgotten language, a burned tongue in a midrash: nobody knows.
God's answer to who am I uses yesterday's word, ehyeh
ki ehyeh imach: I will be with thee.

games.q: you're God, speaking from the bush. the man you've chosen says he can't speak well and begs you to send someone else. what do you do?
o: send him anyway, with his brother to help.
heal his speech on the spot.
games.why: God is angry, but sends him anyway: Aaron will be his mouth. the weakness stays, and Moses goes, not alone.

practice: Think of one thing you're not good at that keeps getting in your way: speaking up, numbers, organizing, asking for things. Don't argue it away; name it honestly, the way Moses did.
Then ask who your Aaron is, someone good at this who might help if you asked, and picture asking them.

wordCard.voice: Ehyeh, I will be, God's answer to Moses' who am I: it's not about you, I will be with you.

orig.note: Hebrew: heavy of mouth, slow of speech. Moses' words about himself.

carryVoice: Your line: slow of speech, still sent. A weakness doesn't cancel a calling. Eighty-three days in.
